The European Ombudsman investigates complaints about maladministration in the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the European Union. Maladministration is understood broadly: it covers not only unlawful acts but also unfairness, unjustified delays, refusal to provide information and failure to reply. The office was created by the Maastricht Treaty, and the first Ombudsman took up duties in 1995; the post-holder is elected by the European Parliament after each European election, for a renewable term matching the Parliament's.

Any citizen or resident of the EU, as well as any company, association or other body with a registered office in a Member State, may lodge a complaint, normally within two years of becoming aware of the problem. The complainant must first have tried to resolve the matter with the institution concerned. Complaints about national, regional or local authorities fall outside the remit, even when those authorities are implementing EU law, and the Court of Justice acting in its judicial role cannot be investigated either.

The Ombudsman cannot issue binding decisions. Instead, the office may propose a solution, make recommendations and, if an institution does not respond satisfactorily, submit a special report to the Parliament. In practice, much of its influence comes from the publicity that such findings attract.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A complaint is still likely to be examined if the complainant has not yet approached the institution concerned.
A complaint that a city council has misapplied an EU directive never falls within the Ombudsman's remit.
If an institution ignores a recommendation, the Ombudsman refers the case to the Court of Justice.
The Ombudsman's influence rests entirely on publicity rather than on any formal procedure.

When the Erasmus programme was launched in 1987, it was designed for students in higher education who wished to spend part of their degree at a university in another participating country. Its name honours the Renaissance scholar Desiderius Erasmus, who studied and taught in several European cities, and it also works as an acronym for the European Community Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students. In its first year, around 3,200 students took part.

In 2014 the programme was merged with several other EU schemes for education, training, youth and sport to form Erasmus+. The new programme kept the familiar brand but widened its audience considerably: apprentices, school pupils, teachers, adult learners and youth workers can now receive support, and funding is available for partnerships between organisations as well as for individual mobility. Its budget for 2021–2027 is substantially larger than that of its predecessor.

Studies commissioned by the European Commission report that former participants tend to find employment more quickly than their peers, although the authors note that students who choose to go abroad may differ from those who do not in ways that also affect their job prospects.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every former participant finds a job sooner than graduates who never studied abroad.
The Erasmus+ budget for 2021–2027 is about twice as large as that of its predecessor.
University students are now likely to be a minority of the people that Erasmus+ supports.
The faster job entry of former participants may partly reflect who chooses to go abroad.

Before adopting the euro, an EU Member State must meet the convergence criteria set out in the Treaties. Its inflation rate must not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points that of the three best-performing Member States in terms of price stability, and its long-term interest rates must not be more than 2 percentage points above those of the same three countries. Its government deficit must not exceed 3% of GDP, and its government debt must not exceed 60% of GDP unless the ratio is diminishing sufficiently and approaching that reference value. Finally, the country must have taken part in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM II) for at least two years without severe tensions, and its national legislation, including the statute of its central bank, must be compatible with the Treaties.

Denmark negotiated an opt-out and is not obliged to adopt the euro. The other Member States outside the euro area are legally committed to joining once they meet the criteria, but because participation in ERM II is voluntary, a country can in practice delay adoption by staying out of the mechanism. Croatia, which met all the criteria, became the twentieth member of the euro area in January 2023.

options: A Member State that has never taken part in ERM II cannot satisfy all the convergence criteria.
Government debt above 60% of GDP usually rules a country out, even when the ratio is falling sufficiently.
Bulgaria followed Croatia into the euro area and became its twenty-first member.
Every Member State outside the euro area is legally obliged to adopt the single currency eventually.

Adopted in 2019, the EU Directive on single-use plastics targets the ten single-use plastic items most often found on European beaches, together with fishing gear. The measures differ according to whether sustainable alternatives exist. Where alternatives are readily available and affordable, products such as plastic cutlery, plates, straws, cotton bud sticks and expanded polystyrene food containers were banned from the EU market from July 2021.

For products without such alternatives, including tobacco filters and wet wipes, the Directive relies on other tools. Member States must reduce the consumption of plastic food containers and drinks cups, and producers of the products concerned must contribute to the costs of waste management and of cleaning up litter under 'extended producer responsibility' schemes. Certain products must also carry a label informing consumers about the plastic they contain and the appropriate way to dispose of them.

Plastic beverage bottles are subject to specific targets: they must contain at least 25% recycled plastic by 2025 for PET bottles and 30% by 2030 for all such bottles, and Member States must collect 77% of them separately by 2025 and 90% by 2029. Since July 2024, caps and lids have had to remain attached to bottles during use.

Wherever an alternative to a plastic product exists, the plastic version has been banned, whatever the price.
Producers of tobacco filters have to help pay for cleaning up the litter their products cause.
Tethered caps have largely solved the problem of bottle lids on European beaches.

Tardigrades, sometimes called water bears, are microscopic animals rarely longer than half a millimetre. More than 1,000 species have been described, living in habitats as varied as deep-sea sediments, Antarctic lakes and the damp moss on city walls. They are famous for surviving conditions that would kill almost any other animal, including extreme cold, intense radiation and prolonged drying out.

Their main survival strategy is a state known as cryptobiosis. As its surroundings dry out, a tardigrade curls into a compact 'tun', loses almost all of its body water and reduces its metabolism to an almost undetectable level. In this state some individuals have revived after years, and in a 2007 experiment some even survived exposure to the vacuum of space. Researchers have also identified proteins that appear to protect tardigrade cells and DNA from damage while they are dried out.

Strictly speaking, however, tardigrades are not extremophiles. They do not thrive in extreme environments; they merely endure them until normal conditions return, and active tardigrades are no more resistant than many other small invertebrates. Most species spend their lives in ordinary, damp habitats.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: More than 1,000 tardigrade species have been shown to survive in the vacuum of space.
Tardigrade proteins will probably allow scientists to store human cells in a dried state.
Their toughness depends largely on the dried-out tun state, not on their active life.
Once in the tun state, a tardigrade survives every hazard it meets, however long it lasts.

Most EU legislation is adopted through the ordinary legislative procedure. The European Commission submits a proposal, and the European Parliament and the Council of the EU act as co-legislators with equal standing: neither can adopt the act without the other. The procedure can involve up to three readings. If the two institutions still disagree after the Parliament's second reading, a conciliation committee with an equal number of representatives from each is convened to draft a joint text, which must then be approved by both. If either rejects it, the proposal falls.

In practice, a large majority of files are now agreed at first reading, often after informal 'trilogue' negotiations between representatives of the Parliament, the Council and the Commission. Trilogues are not provided for in the Treaties, and critics argue that they make it harder for citizens to follow how legislation is shaped, while supporters point to the speed with which agreements are reached.

In the Council, most decisions under the procedure are taken by qualified majority, which requires 55% of Member States representing at least 65% of the EU population. A blocking minority must include at least four Member States.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Three Member States alone never form a blocking minority, however large their combined population.
A joint text drafted by the conciliation committee becomes law once the Parliament has approved it.
The conciliation committee is usually chaired by a representative of the Commission.
Trilogues have shifted influence over EU legislation away from the Parliament and towards the Council.

Around four out of five crop and wildflower species in the EU depend, at least in part, on pollination by animals. Pollinators include not only managed honeybees but also wild bees, hoverflies, butterflies, moths and some beetles, and for several crops wild insects are at least as effective as honeybees. Yet many of these species are in decline: around one in ten bee and butterfly species in Europe is threatened with extinction, and for many others the data are too poor to assess their status.

The main drivers include changes in land use, intensive agricultural practices, pesticide use, invasive alien species, pathogens and climate change. Because these pressures interact, the loss of pollinators is difficult to attribute to any single cause.

In 2018 the European Commission launched the EU Pollinators Initiative, its first dedicated framework to tackle the decline. It focused on improving knowledge of the causes and consequences, tackling the main drivers and raising awareness. A revised initiative adopted in 2023 added actions to restore habitats in farmland and urban areas and to reduce the impact of pesticides, and it set the objective of reversing the decline by 2030.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Wild insects pollinate several crops more effectively than managed honeybees do.
The real share of threatened bee and butterfly species in Europe could be higher than one in ten.
Pesticide use has been identified as the main cause of the decline of European pollinators.
The revised plan will probably succeed in halting pollinator losses by the end of the decade.

The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 in the Luxembourg village of Schengen by five countries: Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. It was followed in 1990 by a convention setting out how internal border controls would be abolished and what common rules would compensate for their removal, including a shared visa policy, police cooperation and a common database, the Schengen Information System. The Schengen rules were incorporated into EU law by the Treaty of Amsterdam in 1999.

The Schengen area today includes most EU Member States as well as four non-EU countries: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Ireland has chosen to remain outside, and Member States that wish to join must first be assessed as applying the rules correctly; their full membership then requires a unanimous decision of the Council.

Although checks at internal borders have been abolished, a member may temporarily reintroduce them as a last resort in the event of a serious threat to public policy or internal security. Such controls must be notified, limited in time and proportionate. Several countries have repeatedly extended controls in recent years, which has led to debate about whether temporary measures have become permanent in practice.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Internal border controls have now become a permanent fixture across Schengen.
The Schengen Information System was mainly set up to process visa applications.
Romania and Bulgaria have both become full members of the Schengen area in recent years.
The end of internal border checks was paired with common measures to compensate for it.

Following its strategy review in 2021, the European Central Bank adopted a symmetric inflation target of 2% over the medium term. Symmetric means that the ECB considers negative deviations from the target as undesirable as positive ones. The previous formulation, which aimed for inflation 'below, but close to, 2%', had been criticised for implying that inflation above 2% was a greater concern than inflation below it, and some economists argued that it had contributed to a period of persistently low inflation.

The medium-term orientation allows the ECB to look through temporary fluctuations, for example in energy prices, rather than react to every monthly change. When interest rates are close to their lower bound, the strategy states that especially forceful or persistent policy measures may be needed to prevent negative deviations from becoming entrenched, which may also imply a transitory period in which inflation is moderately above target.

The review also concluded that the measure of inflation should in future include the costs of owner-occupied housing, which the existing index largely leaves out. Fiscal policy, such as decisions on taxation and public spending, remains the responsibility of national governments.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Under its current strategy the ECB regards inflation above 2% as more harmful than inflation below it.
With interest rates near their lower bound, the ECB may accept inflation moderately above 2% for a while.
The previous formulation was probably the main reason why euro-area inflation stayed low for years.
The ECB's medium-term orientation means that it never reacts to changes in energy prices.

On 9 May 1950, French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman proposed placing French and West German coal and steel production under a common High Authority, within an organisation open to the participation of other European countries. Coal and steel were the raw materials of armaments, and the aim was to make war between historic rivals 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. The plan had been prepared largely by Jean Monnet, who became the first president of the High Authority.

The Treaty of Paris, signed in 1951 by six countries (Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands), established the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC). The United Kingdom was invited to take part but declined, unwilling to transfer control of its industries to a supranational body. Unlike most later treaties, the Treaty of Paris was concluded for a limited period of fifty years; it expired in 2002, and the ECSC's remaining activities and assets were taken over by the European Community.

Today, 9 May is celebrated as Europe Day in recognition of Schuman's declaration, rather than of the signature of any treaty.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Britain refused to let a supranational body take control of its industries.
The ECSC came to an end because its members voted to merge it into the European Community.
The High Authority is often seen as the direct forerunner of today's European Commission.
Jean Monnet prepared the plan behind the Schuman declaration entirely on his own.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) sets rules for online intermediaries such as marketplaces, social networks, app stores and search engines. All providers must meet basic obligations, for example stating in their terms and conditions any restrictions they place on content and how they moderate it. Hosting services, including online platforms, must also offer easy ways to report illegal content and explain to users why their content has been removed or restricted. Online platforms may not show adverts based on profiling to users they know to be minors, and they may not target advertising using sensitive data such as religion or sexual orientation.

Platforms and search engines with at least 45 million monthly active users in the EU, roughly 10% of its population, are designated 'very large' and face additional obligations. They must assess the systemic risks their services pose, for example to elections or public health, take measures to reduce them, submit to independent audits and give vetted researchers access to data. Small and micro enterprises are exempt from some of the obligations that apply to other platforms.

The European Commission supervises very large services directly, while national 'digital services coordinators' oversee other providers. Breaches can lead to fines of up to 6% of the provider's global annual turnover, and repeated serious breaches can lead to a temporary suspension of the service in the EU.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every breach of the DSA exposes the provider to a temporary suspension of its service in the EU.
Platforms must not show profiling-based adverts to any minor, even one whose age they have no way of knowing.
A platform with 40 million active users a month in the EU answers to a national coordinator.
Small platforms are generally exempt from the ban on profiling-based adverts to children.

The European Union has 24 official languages. Under the EU's language rules, any citizen may write to an EU institution in any of these languages and is entitled to receive a reply in the same language. Regulations and other documents of general application are published in all official languages, and the different language versions of EU legislation are equally authentic: no single version prevails over the others.

Irish became an official language in 2007, but a temporary derogation meant that not all documents had to be translated into Irish; the derogation ended on 1 January 2022. Some languages that are official in a Member State, such as Catalan, Basque and Galician in Spain, are not official EU languages, although under administrative arrangements citizens may write to some institutions in them at their own government's expense.

Within the European Commission, day-to-day internal work is carried out mainly in English, French and German, which are often called 'procedural languages'. The European Parliament, by contrast, provides interpretation into all official languages in plenary sessions, reflecting the principle that elected members must be able to work in their own language.

options: English, French and German became procedural languages because they are the EU's most widely spoken languages.
Where language versions of a regulation differ, the English version generally prevails.
Catalan is expected to become an official EU language once Spain's request has been approved.
Unlike a citizen writing in Irish, one writing in Basque has no guaranteed right to a reply in that language.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites change over time and no longer respond to the medicines designed to kill them. It is a natural process, but it is accelerated by the overuse and misuse of antimicrobials in both human medicine and animal husbandry. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control estimates that infections with antibiotic-resistant bacteria cause more than 35,000 deaths each year in the EU and EEA.

Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections such as colds and influenza, yet they are still frequently taken for them, sometimes because patients expect a prescription and sometimes because doctors cannot quickly rule out a bacterial infection. Faster diagnostic tests could therefore reduce unnecessary use, although they are not yet available for many conditions.

In farming, the EU banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feed in 2006, and since 2022 it has also restricted their routine preventive use in groups of healthy animals. Developing new antibiotics is scientifically difficult and commercially unattractive, because new drugs that work against resistant bacteria are likely to be held in reserve and sold in small quantities.

options: Since 2022 the EU has banned all use of antibiotics in groups of healthy farm animals.
If antimicrobials were never overused or misused, resistance to them would not develop at all.
Faster diagnostic tests would largely end the use of antibiotics against colds and influenza.
New drugs against resistant bacteria are likely to sell poorly, which deters developers.

The European Climate Law, adopted in 2021, made the EU's objective of climate neutrality by 2050 legally binding. Climate neutrality means that any remaining greenhouse gas emissions are balanced by removals, for example by forests, soils or carbon capture technologies, so that net emissions are zero. The objective applies to the Union as a whole rather than to each Member State individually, and after 2050 the EU is to aim for negative emissions.

The Law also sets an intermediate target: by 2030, net greenhouse gas emissions must be reduced by at least 55% compared with 1990 levels. Because the target is expressed in net terms, removals count towards it, but the Law caps their contribution so that the target cannot be met mainly by relying on natural sinks. It also created a European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate Change, an independent body that advises on measures and targets.

Critics argued that the 55% target was not ambitious enough to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement, while some industry groups warned that it would raise costs. The Commission must assess progress every five years and can issue recommendations to Member States whose measures it considers inconsistent with the objective.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The EU could meet its 2030 target mainly by planting new forests instead of cutting its emissions.
The 2050 objective does not oblige every Member State to reach net zero on its own territory.
The 55% reduction target is ambitious enough to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement.
The 55% target for 2030 was set by the Scientific Advisory Board, not by the Climate Law.

Galileo is the European Union's global satellite navigation system. Unlike the American GPS and the Russian GLONASS, which were developed under military control, Galileo was designed from the start as a civilian system, although it also offers an encrypted service reserved for government-authorised users such as emergency services and the armed forces. It began offering initial services in December 2016, after years of delays and cost increases.

Galileo is interoperable with GPS, so receivers can combine signals from both constellations, which improves accuracy and availability, particularly in cities where tall buildings block part of the sky. Most smartphones sold in Europe now support Galileo signals. In addition to positioning and timing, the system supports a search and rescue service that helps locate people in distress and, unlike earlier systems, can send a return message confirming that an alert has been received.

Because Galileo is owned by the EU, its signals do not depend on decisions taken by another country, an argument often used to justify its cost. Precise timing signals from satellite systems are also used to synchronise telecommunications networks, energy grids and financial transactions.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Using Galileo with GPS gives more reliable positioning among tall buildings.
Galileo offers no service whose use is restricted to particular categories of users.
Galileo generally provides more accurate positioning than the American GPS does.
Without Galileo, European energy grids and financial systems would be unable to operate.

Research on learning consistently finds that retrieval practice, which means actively recalling information, for instance by testing oneself, leads to better long-term retention than simply rereading material. The benefit appears even when the test is not marked and no feedback is given, although feedback increases it further. Curiously, learners often feel less confident after retrieval practice than after rereading, because recalling information is effortful and exposes gaps, and many therefore prefer the less effective method.

A related finding concerns timing. Spreading study sessions over days or weeks, known as spaced practice, tends to produce more durable learning than concentrating the same amount of study into one session. 'Cramming' can improve performance in a test taken shortly afterwards, but the material is forgotten more quickly. The best gap between sessions seems to depend on how long the information needs to be remembered.

Some researchers also recommend 'interleaving', which means mixing different types of problem within a session instead of practising one type at a time. Interleaving feels harder and initially produces more errors, but in several studies it improved learners' ability to recognise which method a new problem requires.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Cramming can improve scores in a test taken soon afterwards because it reduces anxiety.
Retrieval practice only helps learners when they are told whether their answers are right.
How confident learners feel can be a misleading guide to which study method works best.
Spaced practice works best when the study sessions are held exactly one week apart.

The European Capital of Culture initiative was launched in 1985 on the suggestion of Greek culture minister Melina Mercouri, and Athens was the first city to hold the title. Today, two cities in different EU Member States hold it each year, and every third year a third city from a candidate country, a potential candidate or a member of the European Free Trade Association that belongs to the European Economic Area is also designated.

Cities are not simply appointed. They compete in national selection rounds, a panel of independent experts recommends the winners, and the cities are formally designated four years before the title year, after which their preparations are monitored. The title itself comes with only a modest EU prize, named after Melina Mercouri, which is paid if the city fulfils its commitments; most of the funding comes from national, regional and local budgets and from private sponsors.

Evaluations suggest that the title can boost tourism and urban regeneration, as in Glasgow in 1990 and Lille in 2004, but that the benefits are uneven: some cities struggled to maintain cultural activity once the year was over, and others were criticised for spending heavily on buildings rather than on local cultural participation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Whether the EU prize is paid depends on whether the city fulfils its commitments.
Holding the title guarantees lasting economic benefits for the city that is chosen.
Every year three cities hold the title, one of them from outside the EU.
The Melina Mercouri Prize is worth €1.5 million to each city that receives it.

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) was adopted in 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. It covers organisations established in the EU and also organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. Personal data may be processed only on one of the legal bases the Regulation lists, of which consent is just one; others include the performance of a contract and compliance with a legal obligation.

When a personal data breach is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms, the organisation responsible must notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. The individuals affected must also be informed if the risk is high. Infringements can be punished with fines of up to €20 million or 4% of the company's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

Organisations operating in several Member States generally deal with a single 'lead' supervisory authority in the country of their main establishment. Critics have argued that this concentrates enforcement against large technology companies in a few countries, slowing down major cases.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every personal data breach must be reported to each of the people whose data were affected.
Ireland's data protection authority handles most of the cases against large technology firms.
Under the GDPR, all processing of personal data requires the consent of the person concerned.
A firm with a worldwide annual turnover of €1 billion faces a maximum fine of €40 million.

Natura 2000 is a network of protected areas covering Europe's most valuable and threatened species and habitats. It is the largest coordinated network of protected areas in the world, covering around 18% of the EU's land area and more than 8% of its marine territory. The network is based on two pieces of legislation: the Birds Directive of 1979 and the Habitats Directive of 1992. Member States propose sites, and those designated under the Habitats Directive are selected on the basis of scientific criteria in consultation with the European Commission.

Natura 2000 sites are not strict nature reserves. Much of the land is privately owned, and human activities, including farming, forestry and tourism, are not banned; they must, however, be managed so that they do not harm the species and habitats the sites are designated to protect. Any plan or project likely to have a significant effect on a site must undergo an 'appropriate assessment', and it may be approved despite a negative assessment only for imperative reasons of overriding public interest and if compensatory measures are taken.

Assessments by the European Environment Agency show that, despite the network's size, the conservation status of many protected habitats remains poor.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Sites under the Birds Directive are selected by the Commission on scientific criteria.
Natura 2000 covers a larger area of land in Spain than in any other Member State.
A negative appropriate assessment does not by itself rule out a new road through a site.
Landowners within Natura 2000 sites may farm their land in whatever way they choose.

Under EU rules on air passenger rights, travellers may be entitled to fixed compensation of €250, €400 or €600, depending on the distance of the flight, if their flight is cancelled less than 14 days before departure. The rules themselves do not expressly grant compensation for delays. However, in 2009 the Court of Justice of the EU ruled that passengers who reach their final destination three hours or more late are entitled to the same compensation as for a cancellation.

No compensation is due if the airline can prove that the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken, such as severe weather or air-traffic-control strikes. Technical problems discovered during routine maintenance have generally not been accepted as extraordinary. Separately from compensation, airlines must provide meals, refreshments and, where necessary, hotel accommodation while passengers wait, whatever the cause of the disruption.

The rules cover all flights departing from an EU airport, and flights arriving in the EU from a non-EU country when operated by an EU airline. A revision proposed by the Commission in 2013, which would among other changes raise the delay thresholds, has been the subject of long negotiations.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A flight from New York to Paris operated by a US airline is covered by these EU rules.
A storm that rules out compensation never cancels the duty to provide meals and refreshments.
Any technical fault on an aircraft entitles passengers to compensation under these rules.
The delay needed for compensation has now been raised from three hours to five hours.

The European Citizens' Initiative, introduced by the Treaty of Lisbon and available since 2012, allows citizens to invite the European Commission to propose legislation in an area where the EU has the power to act. An initiative must be organised by a group of at least seven citizens living in seven different Member States, and it must collect at least one million signatures within twelve months. The signatures must come from at least seven Member States, and in each of those a minimum number must be reached: the country's number of Members of the European Parliament multiplied by the total number of Members.

Before collection begins, the Commission checks whether the proposed initiative is admissible; it can refuse to register initiatives that manifestly fall outside its powers or are abusive or frivolous. Once an initiative has collected enough verified signatures, the organisers meet the Commission and present it at a public hearing in the European Parliament.

The Commission must then set out, within six months, what action it intends to take, if any, and its reasons. It is not obliged to propose legislation, and only a handful of the initiatives that reached one million signatures have led directly to new laws, which has led some observers to question the instrument's effectiveness.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: However many signatures are gathered, support from only six Member States would never be enough.
Once an initiative has succeeded, the Commission is obliged to propose a new law within six months.
The Commission itself verifies the signatures before the organisers present the initiative.
The instrument has largely failed, as few successful initiatives have led directly to new laws.

National courts are the ordinary courts of EU law: they apply it in the cases that come before them. When a national court is unsure how a provision of EU law should be interpreted, or whether an act of an EU institution is valid, it may refer a question to the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). A court against whose decisions there is no judicial remedy under national law, typically a supreme court, is in principle obliged to make such a reference, although the CJEU has accepted exceptions, for example where the correct interpretation is so obvious as to leave no reasonable doubt.

The CJEU does not decide the dispute itself. It answers the question referred, and the national court then applies that answer to the facts of the case. Its interpretation binds not only the referring court but also other national courts dealing with the same issue. Only the CJEU can declare an EU act invalid; national courts may reject arguments that an act is invalid, but they cannot set it aside on their own authority.

The procedure has produced many of the landmark rulings that shaped EU law, including those establishing the principles of direct effect and primacy.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A court of last instance must refer every question of EU law, however obvious the answer is.
Once it has answered the question, the CJEU goes on to settle the national dispute itself.
A national judge who doubts an EU regulation's validity is never entitled to set it aside alone.
Lower courts probably refer questions less often than supreme courts, as they are not obliged to.

The European Court of Auditors, based in Luxembourg, is the EU's independent external auditor. Despite its name, it is not a court of law and has no judicial powers. It checks that EU funds are correctly accounted for, raised and spent in accordance with the rules, and that they achieve value for money. It has one member from each Member State, appointed by the Council for a renewable six-year term after consulting the European Parliament.

Each year the Court publishes an annual report on the implementation of the EU budget, including an estimate of the level of error in spending. An error does not necessarily mean that money has been lost or misused: it often reflects payments that did not fully comply with the rules, for example because of procurement mistakes or missing documents. The Court also publishes special reports on specific policies and programmes.

When its auditors detect suspected fraud, they pass the information to the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), which can investigate, or to the European Public Prosecutor's Office. The Parliament, on a recommendation from the Council, decides each year whether to approve the Commission's management of the budget, a procedure known as discharge, in which the Court's findings play an important part.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: OLAF has recovered most of the EU money that the Court identified as lost through fraud.
The Court's findings alone determine whether the Commission is granted discharge each year.
Most errors detected by the Court are probably caused by missing documents, not fraud.
Spending that the Court reports as erroneous may not have involved any loss of EU money.

The EU's long-term budget, the multiannual financial framework (MFF), sets the maximum annual amounts that the Union may spend in each broad policy area over a period of at least five years; the current framework covers 2021–2027. The MFF regulation is adopted by the Council acting unanimously, after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament. Annual budgets, adopted jointly by the Parliament and the Council, must then stay within its ceilings.

The budget is financed mainly from 'own resources': customs duties on imports from outside the EU, a share of the value added tax collected by Member States, a contribution based on non-recycled plastic packaging waste, and contributions based on each Member State's gross national income (GNI). The GNI-based resource is by far the largest source of revenue, which is one reason why debates about the budget often focus on what each country pays in and receives back.

Unlike national governments, the EU may not run a deficit in its annual budget. To finance the NextGenerationEU recovery instrument, however, the Member States authorised the Commission to borrow on the capital markets on an exceptional and temporary basis, with repayment planned until 2058.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Customs duties on imports from outside the EU probably bring in more revenue than any other source.
Any one Member State is in a position to block the adoption of a new multiannual framework.
The EU's annual budget amounts to roughly one per cent of the Union's gross national income.
Debates about the budget are entirely about what each Member State pays in and gets back.

The Council of the EU, where national ministers meet, is chaired by a Member State presidency that rotates every six months in an order fixed in advance. To ensure continuity, the three presidencies that follow each other work together as a 'trio' on a common 18-month programme. The presidency's role is to organise meetings, broker compromises between Member States and represent the Council in negotiations with the European Parliament; it is expected to act as a neutral broker rather than to push its own national interests. The Foreign Affairs Council is an exception: it is chaired by the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.

The European Council, which brings together the heads of state or government, is a separate institution. It has a permanent president, elected by its members by qualified majority for a term of two and a half years, renewable once. The president chairs its meetings and represents the EU externally on foreign and security matters at that level, without prejudice to the powers of the High Representative. The European Council defines the EU's general political directions and priorities but does not exercise legislative functions.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The longest anyone is allowed to serve as President of the European Council is five years.
Presidencies held by smaller Member States tend to be more successful at brokering compromises.
The rotating presidency chairs every configuration of the Council of the EU without exception.
The President of the European Council is solely responsible for representing the EU abroad.

The Council of Europe is often confused with EU bodies, but it is a separate international organisation. Founded in 1949 and based in Strasbourg, it has 46 member states, including all 27 EU Member States; Russia was expelled in 2022. Its best-known achievement is the European Convention on Human Rights, whose application is overseen by the European Court of Human Rights, also in Strasbourg. Individuals who have exhausted the remedies available in their own country can bring a complaint against a state that is party to the Convention.

By contrast, the European Council and the Council of the EU are institutions of the European Union, and the Court of Justice of the EU, which ensures that EU law is interpreted and applied uniformly, sits in Luxembourg. The two systems nevertheless interact: the EU's Charter of Fundamental Rights states that rights corresponding to those in the Convention have the same meaning and scope, and the Treaty of Lisbon requires the EU itself to accede to the Convention, a process that has dragged on for years and is not yet complete. The Council of Europe and the EU also share the same flag, twelve gold stars on a blue background.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights simply reproduces the European Convention on Human Rights.
Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe in 2022 following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Most complaints to the court in Strasbourg are brought against countries that are EU Member States.
Every EU Member State belongs to the Council of Europe, but the EU itself has not yet joined the Convention.

To join the EU, a country must meet the accession criteria defined by the European Council in Copenhagen in 1993. These require stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities; a functioning market economy able to cope with competitive pressure and market forces within the Union; and the ability to take on the obligations of membership, including the capacity to implement EU law effectively. The EU's own capacity to absorb new members while maintaining the momentum of integration is also an important consideration.

Accession negotiations cannot start until all Member States agree, and they are conducted in clusters of chapters covering areas such as competition, the environment and justice. Since 2020 the 'fundamentals', including the rule of law and the functioning of democratic institutions, are opened first and closed last, so that progress on them sets the pace of the negotiations as a whole. Negotiations on any chapter can be halted if the candidate's reforms stall or go into reverse.

When negotiations are complete, the accession treaty must be approved by the Council unanimously, consented to by the European Parliament and ratified by every Member State and by the candidate country.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Once accession talks have opened, they continue whatever happens to the candidate's reforms.
Most candidates are likely to need more than ten years to complete their accession talks.
Every Member State has a veto over both the opening of talks and the final accession treaty.
The EU's capacity to absorb new members is the decisive test of any country's application.

Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union, introduced by the Treaty of Lisbon, allows a Member State to withdraw from the Union in accordance with its own constitutional requirements. The state concerned notifies the European Council of its intention, and the EU then negotiates a withdrawal agreement with it, taking account of the framework for its future relationship with the Union. The agreement is concluded by the Council acting by qualified majority, after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament; the withdrawing state does not take part in the Council's discussions on its own departure.

The Treaties cease to apply to that state from the date the agreement enters into force or, failing that, two years after the notification, unless the European Council, in agreement with the state concerned, unanimously decides to extend this period. A state that has left may later ask to rejoin, but it must then go through the ordinary accession procedure like any other candidate.

The United Kingdom was the first country to use the procedure. It notified its intention in March 2017 and, after the deadline had been extended three times, left the EU on 31 January 2020. A transition period, during which EU law continued to apply to it, lasted until the end of that year.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A withdrawal agreement must be approved unanimously by the remaining Member States in the Council.
Without an agreement, departure can be put off beyond two years only if the European Council agrees unanimously.
The UK's transition period could have been extended had both sides agreed to this in 2020.
The withdrawing state is excluded from all Council business while its departure is negotiated.

Euro banknotes are identical across the euro area, whereas euro coins have a common side and a national side chosen by the issuing country. All coins in circulation can be used anywhere in the euro area, whatever their national side. Each year, euro-area countries may also issue two commemorative €2 coins, which are legal tender throughout the area, as well as collector coins, which are legal tender only in the issuing country and are not intended for circulation.

The European Central Bank has the exclusive right to authorise the issue of euro banknotes; in practice they are issued by the ECB and the national central banks. Coins are issued by the national authorities, but the ECB approves the volume of coins they may issue each year. Several small states outside the EU, such as Monaco, San Marino and the Vatican City, use the euro under formal agreements with the EU and may issue a limited number of their own coins. A few other territories use the euro without any such agreement.

Since 2019 the ECB and the national central banks have no longer issued €500 banknotes, although existing ones remain legal tender. In some euro-area countries, cash payments are rounded so that one- and two-cent coins are rarely needed.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: €500 notes issued before 2019 will probably lose their status as legal tender in the coming years.
Every euro coin issued by a euro-area country is legal tender throughout the euro area.
Rounding of cash payments has made one- and two-cent coins unnecessary across the euro area.
A €1 coin issued by Spain for circulation is valid for payment in every euro-area country.

Since June 2017, people travelling in the EU have been able to use their mobile phones abroad at no extra cost under the 'roam like at home' rules: calls, texts and data are charged at domestic rates, deducted from the customer's normal allowance. The rules were extended in 2022 for another ten years and also apply in Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, which belong to the European Economic Area.

Roaming is intended for periodic travel. Operators may apply a fair use policy to prevent abuse, for example when a customer lives permanently in another country or spends most of the time abroad, and in such cases they may charge a small regulated surcharge after warning the customer. For customers on very cheap unlimited data plans, the amount of data available at domestic prices while roaming can also be capped.

Since 2022, customers have also been entitled to the same quality of service abroad as at home where the visited network allows it, and to free access to emergency services. Roaming in other countries, for instance Switzerland or the United Kingdom, is not covered, and calls made from home to another EU country are subject to separate price caps.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A customer on a very cheap unlimited data plan may not get unlimited data at home prices abroad.
The regulated surcharge for fair-use cases is set at the same level in every Member State.
Calls from home to another EU country will probably be charged at domestic rates from 2032.
Since 2022, travellers have been guaranteed the same quality of mobile service abroad as at home.

The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), launched in 2005, works on the 'cap and trade' principle. A cap is set on the total amount of certain greenhouse gases that can be emitted by the installations covered, and the cap is reduced over time so that total emissions fall. Within the cap, companies receive or buy emission allowances, which they can trade with one another. Each year a company must surrender enough allowances to cover all its emissions, or face heavy fines.

The system covers power and heat generation, energy-intensive industry and aviation within Europe, and it was extended to maritime transport from 2024. In its early years, too many allowances were issued and prices collapsed, so a market stability reserve was introduced to absorb the surplus. Some industries at risk of moving production outside the EU have received a share of their allowances free of charge; these free allocations are being phased out as a carbon border adjustment mechanism, which puts a price on the emissions embedded in certain imports, is phased in.

A second, separate system covering fuel used in buildings and road transport is due to start later, and part of its revenues will support vulnerable households.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The market stability reserve was introduced in 2019 to absorb the surplus of allowances.
For some industries, free allowances are giving way to a carbon charge on certain imports.
Shipping firms have probably cut their emissions faster than airlines since joining the ETS.
The existing ETS already covers greenhouse gas emissions from all sectors of the EU economy.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), launched in 1962, is one of the EU's oldest policies and still accounts for a large share of the EU budget. It is organised in two 'pillars'. The first pillar consists mainly of direct payments to farmers, together with market measures, and is financed entirely from the EU budget. The second pillar supports rural development, for example investment in farms, environmental schemes and support for young farmers; unlike the first pillar, it is co-financed by Member States.

Since 2023, each Member State has implemented the CAP through a national strategic plan approved by the Commission, giving governments more freedom to design measures suited to local conditions. A portion of direct payments is reserved for 'eco-schemes', which reward farmers for practices that benefit the climate and the environment, and to receive full support farmers must respect a set of basic standards known as conditionality.

Critics argue that direct payments, which are largely linked to the area farmed, still favour large landowners, with a significant share of the money going to a small proportion of recipients. Supporters reply that the payments stabilise farm incomes, which are often lower and more volatile than incomes in other sectors.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Around a third of the EU's long-term budget is spent on the Common Agricultural Policy.
Direct payments are linked entirely to the area farmed, which is why large landowners benefit.
Unlike rural development, direct payments to farmers are not co-financed by Member States.
Eco-schemes have probably helped to make farm incomes more stable since their introduction.

EU cohesion policy aims to reduce disparities between regions. For the 2021–2027 period, regions are grouped into three categories according to their GDP per inhabitant compared with the EU average. 'Less developed regions' have a GDP per head below 75% of the average; 'transition regions' lie between 75% and 100%; and 'more developed regions' are above 100%. Less developed regions receive the largest share of funding and the highest EU co-financing rates, so that national or regional authorities have to contribute a smaller share of the cost of each project.

In addition, the Cohesion Fund supports Member States, rather than individual regions, whose gross national income per inhabitant is below 90% of the EU average, financing transport networks and environmental projects. Funds are managed jointly: the Commission negotiates partnership agreements and programmes with each country, while national and regional authorities select and monitor projects.

Evaluations generally find that cohesion spending has supported growth in poorer regions, but they also point to persistent problems, including slow absorption of the funds available and administrative capacity that varies greatly between countries. Some regions have remained below 75% of the EU average for decades.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A region whose GDP per head rose from 74% to 76% of the EU average would move into another category.
The Cohesion Fund allocates its money directly to individual regions within the Member States.
Evaluations show that cohesion spending has largely closed the gap between poorer and richer regions.
Absorption of cohesion funds has been slowest in the Member States that joined most recently.

The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is issued free of charge by national health insurance providers. It gives the holder access to medically necessary, state-provided healthcare during a temporary stay in another EU country, as well as in Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, under the same conditions and at the same cost as people insured in that country. If treatment is free for locals, it is free for EHIC holders too; if locals pay a contribution, so do card holders, although they may be able to claim a refund at home.

'Medically necessary' care is care that cannot reasonably wait until the person returns home. It includes treatment for chronic or pre-existing conditions, such as kidney dialysis, although some of these treatments must be arranged in advance with the facility providing them.

The card is not an alternative to travel insurance. It does not cover private healthcare, the cost of returning home after an illness, or lost or stolen property, and it does not cover treatment when the purpose of the trip is to obtain medical care. Travellers are therefore generally advised to take out private travel insurance as well.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Card holders who pay a contribution abroad are always refunded in full by their insurer at home.
The card is issued free of charge and remains valid for five years from the date of issue.
Most travellers who carry the card probably also take out private travel insurance.
A tourist who needs regular dialysis can, with some advance planning, be treated using the card.

REACH, the EU regulation on chemicals that entered into force in 2007, places the burden of proof on industry rather than on public authorities. Companies that manufacture or import a chemical substance in quantities of one tonne or more per year must register it with the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) in Helsinki, providing information on its properties, its uses and how it can be handled safely; the amount of information required increases with the quantity produced. The principle is often summarised as 'no data, no market': a substance that has not been registered cannot be manufactured or placed on the EU market in those quantities.

Substances of very high concern, such as those that cause cancer or accumulate in living organisms, can be placed on a list from which they may be moved to an authorisation list. Once that happens, they can be used only with a specific authorisation, which is granted only if the risks are adequately controlled or if the socio-economic benefits outweigh them and no suitable alternative exists. Certain uses of other substances can also be restricted across the EU.

Environmental organisations argue that identifying and restricting harmful chemicals takes too long, while industry points to the high cost of registration for small companies.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Companies must register every substance they make or import under REACH, whatever the quantity.
A firm producing ten tonnes of a substance a year must supply more data than one producing two.
The cost of registration is likely to have driven a number of small firms out of the EU market.
Any substance found to cause cancer is automatically placed on the authorisation list.

In March 2021, the EU energy label for several household appliances, including fridges, dishwashers, washing machines and televisions, was rescaled. Over the years so many products had reached the top classes that the old A+++ to D scale no longer helped consumers distinguish between them. The new labels use a simpler A to G scale without plus signs, and the top class was deliberately left almost empty when the new scale was introduced, so that it can be filled as technology improves.

Because the requirements for each class were tightened, a product previously rated A+++ might now be rated C or D, even though its energy consumption has not changed. To avoid confusion, retailers had to replace the old labels within a short transition period. The new labels also carry a QR code linking to an EU database with further product information, and some show additional details such as the noise level or the water consumption per cycle.

Other products, such as light sources, were rescaled later, and the rescaling of further categories, including tumble dryers and space heaters, was scheduled for the following years. The label applies to appliances sold in the EU, whether they are manufactured inside or outside it.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every product rated A+++ under the old scale was reclassified as C or D under the new one.
QR codes on the labels have probably led consumers to choose more efficient appliances.
When the new scale was introduced, few if any appliances qualified for its highest class.
All appliance categories sold in the EU were rescaled at the same time in March 2021.

Under an EU directive, USB-C has become the common charging port for a wide range of electronic devices. The requirement has applied to mobile phones, tablets, digital cameras, headphones, handheld video game consoles, portable speakers and similar devices since the end of December 2024, and it applies to laptops from April 2026. Devices that support fast charging must also use a common fast-charging protocol, so that any compatible charger delivers the same speed.

Consumers can also buy a new device without a charger, and packaging must show by means of a pictogram whether a charger is included, together with information about the power the device needs. The Commission expects these measures to reduce electronic waste and to save consumers money, since many households already own several compatible chargers.

Devices that are too small to have a USB-C port, such as smartwatches and some fitness trackers, are not covered. The directive also allows the Commission to update the rules as technology evolves; wireless charging, which is becoming more common, is likely to be the next area for harmonisation.

options: Laptops have been required to have a USB-C port since the end of December 2024.
Since the end of 2024, every electronic device sold in the EU has had to have a USB-C port.
Wireless chargers will probably have to follow a common EU standard from 2028 onwards.
Buyers can tell from a symbol on the packaging whether a charger comes with the device.

Members of the European Parliament are elected every five years by direct universal suffrage. The number of seats per Member State is based on 'degressive proportionality': larger countries have more seats than smaller ones, but smaller countries have more seats per inhabitant. No Member State may have fewer than six or more than 96 seats. Following the 2024 elections, the Parliament had 720 members.

Each country organises the election according to its own rules within a common framework. All countries use a form of proportional representation, but some form a single national constituency while others are divided into regions, and some allow voters to express preferences for individual candidates. The minimum voting age is 18 in most Member States but 16 in some, such as Austria, Belgium, Germany and Malta. EU citizens living in another Member State can vote and stand there, or vote in their home country, but not in both.

Once elected, most MEPs sit in transnational political groups rather than in national delegations. Turnout in European elections fell steadily from 62% in 1979 to about 43% in 2014, before rising to just over 50% in 2019 and 2024.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: On average, MEPs from small Member States represent fewer citizens than those from large ones.
Germany, as the most populous Member State, is the only country holding the maximum of 96 seats.
Turnout tends to be higher in Member States where people are allowed to vote from sixteen.
Because MEPs sit in political groups, national delegations play no part in the Parliament.

The President of the European Commission is proposed by the European Council, acting by qualified majority and taking into account the results of the European Parliament elections. The candidate is then elected by the Parliament by a majority of its component members; if the candidate fails to obtain that majority, the European Council must propose a new candidate within a month. The President-elect, together with the Council, then adopts the list of the other Commissioners, one from each Member State, on the basis of suggestions by national governments.

Each candidate Commissioner appears at a hearing before the relevant parliamentary committee, and committees have on several occasions rejected candidates, forcing governments to nominate someone else. The whole College is then subject to a single vote of consent by the Parliament, after which it is formally appointed by the European Council.

The Parliament can later force the entire Commission to resign by adopting a motion of censure by a two-thirds majority of the votes cast, representing a majority of its members. No motion of censure has ever been adopted, although in 1999 the Santer Commission resigned before a likely vote.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A motion of censure needs the support of two-thirds of all the Members of the Parliament.
The Santer Commission resigned mainly because of allegations of fraud and mismanagement.
Though it votes on the College as a whole, the Parliament has in practice shaped who becomes a Commissioner.
The choice of the Commission President rests solely with the European Parliament.

Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, is based in Warsaw. It supports EU Member States and Schengen-associated countries in managing the EU's external borders, for example by coordinating joint operations, deploying border guards from its standing corps, carrying out risk analysis and assisting with the return of people who have no right to stay. The standing corps, created in 2019, is being built up to a planned 10,000 officers, made up of agency staff and officers seconded by Member States.

However, Member States retain primary responsibility for controlling their own sections of the external border. Frontex staff deployed on a Member State's territory operate under the command of that state, and an operation requires its agreement. The agency may intervene without such a request only in a narrow set of circumstances, and even then the Member State concerned must cooperate.

The agency has a Fundamental Rights Officer and a complaints mechanism, which anyone who believes their rights have been violated during a Frontex operation can use. Reports of alleged pushbacks at the borders have nevertheless led to investigations and to the resignation of its executive director in 2022.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The executive director resigned in 2022 after an OLAF inquiry into alleged pushbacks.
Anyone who thinks Frontex staff violated their rights can complain to the agency.
Frontex can never act on a Member State's territory unless that state has asked it to.
The standing corps is likely to reach its planned strength of 10,000 officers by 2027.

The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO), based in Luxembourg, started operating in June 2021. It is an independent body responsible for investigating, prosecuting and bringing to judgment crimes against the EU's financial interests, such as fraud involving EU funds, corruption and serious cross-border VAT fraud involving damage of at least €10 million.

The EPPO was set up through 'enhanced cooperation', which means that not all Member States take part; in non-participating countries, national authorities remain responsible for these offences, and the EPPO relies on cooperation agreements with them. It works through European Delegated Prosecutors located in the participating Member States, who conduct investigations under the supervision of a central office and bring cases before national courts, applying national criminal procedure.

Before the EPPO existed, the investigation of fraud against the EU budget depended entirely on national prosecutors, whose priorities and resources varied widely, and on the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), which can carry out administrative investigations but cannot prosecute. OLAF continues to exist, and the two bodies are expected to complement each other. In its first years, the EPPO opened investigations into estimated damages running into billions of euros.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Most of the EPPO's investigations so far have concerned fraud involving agricultural subsidies.
Since 2021, the EPPO has prosecuted fraud against the EU budget in all of the Member States.
The EPPO investigates every crime against the EU's financial interests, whatever the damage.
A cross-border VAT fraud causing €5 million of damage is below the EPPO's VAT threshold.

Reef-building corals live in partnership with microscopic algae that live inside their tissues. The algae provide the coral with most of its food through photosynthesis and give it much of its colour. When water temperatures stay unusually high for a prolonged period, corals become stressed and expel the algae, turning white, a process known as bleaching. Heat is the main trigger, but strong sunlight, pollution and changes in salinity can also contribute.

A bleached coral is not dead, and it can recover if conditions return to normal quickly enough for the algae to recolonise its tissues. If the stress continues, however, the coral is likely to starve and die. Even corals that survive may grow and reproduce more slowly for some time and become more vulnerable to disease.

Scientists warn that more frequent marine heatwaves give reefs less time to recover between bleaching events. Some coral species and some individual colonies are more heat-tolerant than others, and researchers are studying whether these could be used to help restore damaged reefs, although they caution that such efforts cannot replace reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A coral that survives bleaching may still be weakened for some time afterwards.
Bleached corals usually recover within a few weeks once the water temperature falls.
Heat is the only factor capable of causing corals to lose their algae and turn white.
More than half of the world's coral reefs have bleached at least once since 2000.

In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould contaminating one of his bacterial cultures had killed the surrounding bacteria. He named the active substance penicillin and published his observations, but he struggled to purify it in useful quantities, and for about a decade the discovery attracted little attention.

At the end of the 1930s, a team at the University of Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed methods to extract and purify the drug, and in 1940 they showed that it protected infected mice. The first human patient they treated, a policeman, improved at first in 1941 but died because supplies ran out before treatment could be completed. Because British industry was stretched by the war, much of the development of large-scale production took place in the United States, where researchers found a more productive strain of mould and better fermentation methods.

By the time of the Normandy landings in 1944, penicillin was available in sufficient quantities to treat Allied troops. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In his Nobel lecture, Fleming warned that bacteria could become resistant if the drug was used in doses that were too low.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Large-scale production of penicillin was developed entirely in the United States.
Fleming's warning about resistance was probably ignored by most doctors at the time.
The first patient most likely died because the drug ran short, not because it failed.
By 1944 penicillin was available in quantities sufficient to treat everyone who needed it.

A heat pump does not generate heat by burning fuel. Instead, it uses electricity to move heat from one place to another, for example from the outside air, the ground or water into a building. Because it moves heat rather than creating it, a heat pump can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity it consumes; this ratio is known as the coefficient of performance.

Air-source heat pumps work even when the outside air is cold, but their efficiency falls as the temperature difference between outside and inside increases. Ground-source systems draw on the more stable temperature below the surface and are therefore more efficient in winter, but they cost more to install because of the drilling or digging required. Heat pumps also work best in well-insulated buildings with large radiators or underfloor heating, because they deliver heat at lower temperatures than gas boilers.

The climate benefit of a heat pump depends partly on how the electricity it uses is generated. The running cost depends on the price of electricity relative to that of gas, which differs considerably between countries; where electricity is expensive, savings on bills can be small even though the heat pump uses less energy overall.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Most new homes in the EU are likely to be built with heat pumps rather than gas boilers.
Installing a heat pump does not guarantee lower energy bills in every country.
Thanks to their efficiency in winter, ground-source heat pumps are the better choice for every household.
Because they deliver heat at lower temperatures, heat pumps cannot work in poorly insulated buildings.

Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night. This 'urban heat island' effect arises because materials such as asphalt, concrete and brick absorb solar heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while buildings, air conditioning and traffic produce additional waste heat. Cities also have less vegetation, so less cooling comes from the evaporation of water from plants and soil, and tall buildings can trap heat and reduce air flow.

During heatwaves the effect increases health risks, especially for older people, young children and people with chronic illnesses, partly because high night-time temperatures prevent the body from recovering from the heat of the day. Within a single city, temperatures can vary considerably between neighbourhoods, and poorer districts with fewer trees are often among the hottest.

Measures such as planting trees, creating parks and green roofs, and using lighter-coloured surfaces that reflect more sunlight can reduce temperatures locally. Air conditioning protects people indoors but releases heat outside and, depending on how the electricity is produced, can add to greenhouse gas emissions, so planners increasingly combine it with passive measures such as shading and ventilation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Green roofs lower city temperatures more effectively than lighter-coloured surfaces.
The poorest districts of a city are always the hottest ones during a heatwave.
Planting trees and creating parks can lower temperatures across an entire city.
Warm nights add to the health risk by denying the body a chance to recover.

The Single European Act, signed in 1986 and in force from 1987, was the first major revision of the Treaties of Rome. Its central aim was to complete the internal market, meaning the free movement of goods, services, people and capital, by the end of 1992. A Commission White Paper published in 1985 had identified around 300 legislative measures needed to remove physical, technical and fiscal barriers between the Member States.

To make this programme possible, the Act extended the use of qualified majority voting in the Council to most single-market legislation, which until then had often required unanimity; tax matters, however, continued to require unanimity. It also strengthened the role of the European Parliament through a new 'cooperation procedure', which gave the Parliament a second reading and made it harder for the Council to ignore its views, and it gave formal recognition to European Political Cooperation in foreign policy.

Not every barrier disappeared by the deadline. Many measures had been adopted by the end of 1992, but some were transposed late into national law, and in several areas, such as services and public procurement, a fully integrated market remained incomplete for years. Even so, the programme is widely credited with reviving European integration after a period of stagnation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The 1985 White Paper was drawn up by the Commission led by Jacques Delors.
After 1987, tax measures could be adopted by a qualified majority in the Council.
From 1987, every Member State still had a veto over Community tax measures.
Thanks to the Act, the internal market was fully completed by the end of 1992.

The Treaty of Lisbon, signed in 2007, entered into force on 1 December 2009 after a difficult ratification, including a second referendum in Ireland. It largely took over the institutional reforms of the Constitutional Treaty, which had been abandoned after being rejected in referendums in France and the Netherlands in 2005, but it dropped constitutional symbols such as an official anthem and flag from the treaty text.

Lisbon made the Charter of Fundamental Rights legally binding, giving it the same legal value as the Treaties, although Poland and the United Kingdom obtained a protocol clarifying how it applied to them. It extended the ordinary legislative procedure, in which the European Parliament and the Council decide on an equal footing, to many new policy areas, and it introduced a new definition of qualified majority based on a 'double majority' of Member States and population, which took effect in 2014.

The European Council became a formal institution of the EU with a permanent president, and the post of High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy was created, combining two previous roles. The European Accessibility Act sets common accessibility requirements for a range of products and services. Horizon Europe is the EU's research and innovation framework programme for 2021–2027, with a budget of around €95 billion. ERC grants are awarded on the sole criterion of scientific excellence, assessed by panels of researchers; there are no thematic priorities and no requirement to form international consortia, and grant holders can be of any nationality provided that the research is carried out in a Member State or an associated country. Success rates are low, typically between about one in ten and one in seven applications.

Most collaborative projects under the second pillar, by contrast, involve partners from several countries and respond to calls defined around policy priorities such as health, climate and digital technology. A small number of AI practices considered to pose an unacceptable risk, such as social scoring or manipulative techniques that exploit people's vulnerabilities, are prohibited. 'High-risk' systems, for example AI used in recruitment, credit scoring, education or medical devices, must meet strict requirements on risk management, data quality, documentation, human oversight and accuracy before they can be placed on the market.

Systems with limited risk are subject mainly to transparency obligations: people must be told, for instance, when they are interacting with a chatbot, and content generated or manipulated by AI, such as deepfakes, must be labelled. Most AI applications, such as spam filters or AI in video games, fall into the minimal-risk category and face no new obligations. Separate rules apply to providers of general-purpose AI models, with additional requirements for the most powerful ones.

Its aim is that losses should be borne first by a bank's shareholders and creditors, through a process known as bail-in, rather than by taxpayers, with a Single Resolution Fund financed by contributions from the banks themselves available as a further backstop.

The third element, a common European deposit insurance scheme, has not been agreed. For now, national deposit guarantee schemes across the EU protect deposits of up to €100,000 per depositor per bank, on the basis of harmonised rules. Supporters of a common scheme argue that it would make all deposits in the banking union equally safe; opponents in some countries are concerned that they would end up paying for the risks of banks elsewhere.
